system:
You are an interpretability researcher. You are given a real pre-trained transformer language model and a set of prompts on which it shows one behaviour. Your job is to work out HOW the model produces that behaviour, internally, and to write it down as a CONSTRUCTION that an automatic judge will test against the model.

WHAT A CONSTRUCTION IS
A short, standalone Python file that defines:

  DESCRIPTION = "plain-language account of the mechanism"

  def model(x, iv):
      # x: the task's inputs, an integer numpy array [B, n_features] (one row per prompt; the columns are described below).
      # Must return the model's predicted output [B, n_answers]: the logits of the task's answer tokens at the end position.
      # Every named intermediate variable is registered with iv:
      #     v = iv("name", value)        value is an array [B] or [B, k]; iv returns it in the same shape.
      # ALWAYS compute later steps from what iv returned, never from a copy made before the iv call:
      # during intervention tests iv returns a replaced value, and your model must respond to it.
      ...

  ALIGN = {"name": ["site", ...], ...}     # for each variable, the site(s) of the network where it lives

The file can use numpy (as np) and math only. It CANNOT see the weights or run the network: every constant it needs (directions' coefficients, thresholds, small tables) must be written into the file as literals, after you have measured them. Limit: 16,000 characters. It is a compact program a person can read, not a copy of the network.

SITES. A site is one vector per prompt, read at one token position:
  resid{L}@p       the residual stream entering block L at position p. resid0 is the token + position embedding; resid{n_layers} is the final residual stream (before the last LayerNorm and the unembedding). So resid{L} is the state after blocks 0..L-1.
  attn{L}@p        what attention layer L adds to the residual stream at p;     head{L}.{H}@p   what its head H adds at p
  mlp{L}@p         what the MLP of layer L adds at p;                           neur{L}@p       its hidden neurons at p (after GELU)
  pattern{L}.{H}@p the attention weights of head H of layer L from position p to every position
p is one of the task's role names (given below) or a token index (0, 1, ..., -1 for the last).

HOW THE JUDGE TESTS A CONSTRUCTION (on prompts held out from fitting)
1. Behaviour: does model(x) pick the same answer token (largest output) as the network?
2. Alignment: at each site in ALIGN the judge fits ONE affine map from the variables you placed there to the real activations (activation = c + variables @ M). So a variable must be related to the activations linearly. A quantity the network encodes through several nonlinear functions of it (a one-hot code, a few smooth or periodic functions, a few measured coordinates) should be those functions' values, a few coordinates, not the raw quantity.
3. CUTS. All residual sites you name at one depth L (resid{L}@p for several p) are tested TOGETHER as "cut{L}": the state of the computation at depth L.
   - Substitution: the named positions are replaced by your prediction (c + variables @ M) and EVERY OTHER position at that depth by its mean over the prompts; the rest of the network runs. The answers must survive (90%). So a cut must name every position that still matters at that depth, with variables that carry everything the later layers use from it. Positions that hold nothing the later layers need can be left out.
   - Necessity: removing the named subspace from the real activations must destroy the answers.
   - Compactness: the judge reports how many principal components of the cut suffice to keep 99% of the answers; the non-categorical variables you name may have at most about twice that many dimensions in total.
     CATEGORICAL variables are exempt from this limit: the IDENTITY of one token or one quantity may be given as a one-hot vector (np.eye(K)[value]), provided each value occurs in at least 6 prompts on average (so "which number is at position n2" is fine; a one-hot of the whole input is not). A compact code with a few features (periodic, digit-wise, monotone ...) is a stronger result when you can find one, but an identity is a legitimate variable: what matters is where it lives, and what the network computes from it.
   - Interchange: the network is run on prompt B, but the part of the cut that encodes your variables is replaced by what it is on prompt A; the network's new answer must equal what model(B) returns when iv gives those variables their values from A (90%). So the causal wiring of model() must mirror the network.
   - Partial / edit, states that no prompt produces (50% of the cases where the network's answer changes; passing either is enough): partial copies ONE variable from A while the cut's other variables stay as in B; edit copies a random half of the coordinates of everything named (not run on one-hot variables). Give each separately-stored part its own variable (one per position, per feature group). These tests put the network in states such as "the tokens of B, but with variable v as in A", so model() must say what the network does with ANY combination of its variables' values, not only the combinations the prompts contain: find that out by patching (hook) before you write it down.
   Sites of the other kinds (attn, mlp, head, neur, pattern) are tested one at a time with the same tests. They say which component carries a variable; they are welcome detail, but only cuts count toward completeness.
4. STAGES. The model's depth is divided into stages: the embedding (resid0), then four bands of layers (for 12 layers: resid1-3, resid4-6, resid7-9, resid10-12). A stage is explained when one cut inside it is verified. The construction is COMPLETE when it behaves like the network and every stage has a verified cut: it then says what the network holds, where, from the tokens to the answer, and model() says how each stage's variables are computed from the previous stage's. That is the goal, reached one stage at a time.

YOUR TOOLS
- python(code): a persistent session (variables stay between calls). Defined:
    X [N, n_features] the task inputs; X_NAMES; PROMPTS (list of N strings); TOKENS [N, T] token ids; ROLES {role: token position}; ANSWERS (the answer tokens, strings); ANSWER_IDS
    run(x, hook=None) -> [B, n_answers]: the network's answer logits for task prompts. x = rows of X, or a 1-D array of prompt numbers.
    logits(x, hook=None) -> [B, n_vocab]: all logits at the end position.
    acts(x, sites) -> {site: array [B, width]} for the site names you ask for.
    hook = {site: array [B, width] (or [width]) or function(array) -> array}: the run is done with those activations REPLACED. This is how you do your own experiments: mean-ablate a site, patch it from other prompts (acts on prompts A, run on prompts B with hook), add a direction, swap a subspace. Several sites can be hooked at once. "resid{L}@*" addresses all positions at once, flattened [B, T * d_model].
    run_tokens(tokens [B, T'], hook=None, sites=()) -> (logits [B, n_vocab] at the last position, {site: array}): any token sequences, not only the task's prompts (positions in site names must be token indices). tok(text) -> token ids; detok(ids) -> token strings.
    W: dict of the weights (numpy): W_E [n_vocab, d], W_pos, W_U [d, n_vocab], ln_f.w/b, and per layer l: L{l}.W_Q, W_K, W_V [n_heads, d, d_head], b_Q, b_K, b_V, W_O [n_heads, d_head, d], b_O, ln1.w/b, ln2.w/b, W_in [d, d_mlp], b_in, W_out [d_mlp, d], b_out. CFG: sizes.
    unembed(v) -> logits for final-residual vector(s) v (applies the last LayerNorm); top(vocab_vector, k) -> the k largest tokens.
    np, scipy, sklearn. Print what you want to see; output is cut at about 8,000 characters, so print summaries, not raw arrays.
  Cost: a run over 200 prompts takes about 0.2-1 s (less when the hooked sites are late in the network and at late positions). A call is stopped after 600 s: plan scans (for example every layer at a few positions first, heads only where it matters), and use a subset of a few hundred prompts.
- submit(code): sends a construction file to the judge and returns its report (it takes a minute or two). The report is the fastest way to learn what is right: unit by unit, variable by variable, what passes and what fails, next to controls.

SUBMIT EARLY, THEN IMPROVE STAGE BY STAGE
Do not try to understand everything before you submit. A construction with one cut is a valid submission, and partial constructions are expected. Make your first submission within your first 8 steps. After that, submit whenever you have changed something; if you go 6 steps without submitting you will be required to submit what you have. WORK BACKWARDS FROM THE ANSWER: first the last stage (what the end position holds just before the unembedding), then the stage before it (what must be present, and at which positions, for the last stage's variables to be computed), and so on down. Each stage you verify tells you what the stage below has to deliver. Leave the embedding stage for LAST: it is usually the hardest, because its partial tests ask what the model does when one input token is exchanged for another, which needs a full model of the behaviour off the prompts. Do not spend many steps on one failing stage while a later stage is still unverified. Keep verified cuts in every submission; a cut that fails costs judge time, so include only the failing cut you are working on.

HOW TO WORK
1. Find out WHAT the model does on these prompts: which answer it picks as a function of x. Write model(x) for the behaviour first.
2. Find out WHERE the information is at each depth. For a depth L and each position, replace resid{L}@p by its mean (or patch it from another prompt) and see whether the answers change: that gives the positions a cut at L must name, and how information moves between positions across depth. Patching from a prompt that differs in ONE input quantity shows where that quantity lives.
3. Find out WHAT is held there: variables that are functions of x and that the site's activations are a linear function of. Check candidates by regression, and check that they are the part that matters by running the network with the site replaced by your regression's prediction (this is the judge's substitution test; do it yourself before submitting). For a quantity with many values (a token's identity, a number), look at how the activations vary with it: principal components of the per-value means, periodic or monotone structure along the value, digit structure; use the few coordinates that carry the behaviour. Look at the weights too: the embedding and unembedding rows of the tokens involved, which heads' QK attend where and what their OV writes, which directions an MLP reads and writes. Let the numbers decide; do not assume a mechanism because it is familiar.
4. Write the construction: variables at each cut, each computed in model() from the previous cut's variables (or from x at the embedding), the answer logits computed from the last ones. Measure the constants with python and write them into the file. Submit, read the report, fix what fails.
5. If a unit fails, find out why with python before resubmitting (what does the cut depend on that your variables miss? which position did you leave out? is the variable used by the later layers at that depth at all?). You can reproduce every judge test yourself with run, acts and hook.
Keep each message short. Do the thinking with code. When the judge reports VERIFIED AND COMPLETE, or you are certain you cannot improve further, reply with a short final summary and no tool call.
task:
THE NETWORK
gpt2: a pre-trained decoder-only transformer language model (12 layers, 12 heads per layer, d_model 768, d_head 64, d_mlp 3072, vocabulary 50257; pre-LayerNorm blocks: resid += attn(ln1(resid)); resid += mlp(ln2(resid)); logits = ln_f(resid) @ W_U; learned absolute position embeddings; GELU).

THE PROMPTS (2880 prompts, each 5 tokens)
Each prompt is "<month1> <year> - <month2>", a date range whose end year is to be predicted, for example "March 1987 - January". x[:, 0] = month1 and x[:, 1] = month2 as indices 0..11 (0 = January ... 11 = December); x[:, 2] = the year (1980..1999). Every pair of months occurs with every year. Token positions: 0 <|endoftext|>, 1 month1, 2 the year, 3 " -", 4 month2 (the last token). Roles: m1 = 1, year = 2, dash = 3, m2 = end = 4. The network's output is three logits at the end position: of the year token itself ("same year"), of the next year ("next year") and of the year before ("previous year"); these tokens differ from prompt to prompt.
Examples: '<|endoftext|>January 1980 - January' | '<|endoftext|>May 1983 - January' | '<|endoftext|>September 1986 - January' | '<|endoftext|>January 1990 - January' | '<|endoftext|>May 1993 - January' | '<|endoftext|>September 1996 - January'
Features (columns of x): m1, m2, year.
Roles (token positions): dash = 3, m1 = 1, m2 = 4, year = 2, end = 4.
Answer tokens (3): 'same year', 'next year', 'previous year'.

SITES: resid0..resid12, and attn / mlp / neur for layers 0..11, head / pattern for heads 0..11, each @ a role or a token index.
STAGES: embedding; layers 0-2; layers 3-5; layers 6-8; layers 9-11.

You are not told what the model does on these prompts. Find out.

Begin.

import numpy as np

DESCRIPTION = """Rough first pass. The task is to predict the year token that follows "m1 YYYY - m2":
the answer is one of three year tokens (same year, next year, previous year). What I have
established so far: mean-ablating the end position (position 4) at any depth destroys the
answer (0.35-0.74 survival), the year token at position 2 matters until late (still 0.89 at
resid10@2, 0.97 at resid11@2), and position 1 (m1) stops mattering after layer ~8
(resid8@1 ablated: answers survive 1.00). So the end-position residual at depth 12 is the
place where the answer-year decision lives, and the 'which year number' part is copied from
position 2 by late-layer attention. The behaviour is mostly 'next year' with a switch to
'same year' as the second month gets late in the year, so the first draft encodes a single
month-order scalar at the final residual and reads the three answer logits off it."""

def model(x, iv):
    m1 = x[:, 0].astype(float)
    m2 = x[:, 1].astype(float)
    # single scalar: how much earlier m2 is than m1 (drives 'next year')
    s = iv("month_order", (m1 - m2) / 11.0)
    z = 2.0 * s
    out = np.stack([np.zeros_like(z), z, -z], axis=1)
    return out

ALIGN = {"month_order": ["resid12@end"]}

import numpy as np

DESCRIPTION = """The answer logits of the three year tokens are (verified to 2e-4) exactly the last
LayerNorm of resid12 at the end position (position 4 = the second month) dot the unembedding rows
of year-1, year, year+1. So the whole decision lives in resid12@end and is an affine functional of
it: only the two differences next-same and prev-same matter. Decomposing those differences over the
writes into position 4 shows the decision is built there: mlp9@4 contributes +1.05 (of the mean),
mlp10@4 +0.45, attn8@4 -0.25, and nothing else contributes much; the year itself does not move
during layers 9-11 (mean-ablating position 2 at resid10/resid11 keeps 89%/97% of the answers).
The construction therefore models the last stage as two numbers held at resid12@end: T = logit(next)
- logit(same) and U = logit(prev) - logit(same), computed here with an additive table in m1, m2 and
year (a first approximation: it explains about half of T's variance; the rest is a month-by-year
interaction I have not yet traced). U is negative everywhere, so 'previous year' never wins."""

# additive tables measured on the prompts (main effects of m1, m2 and year on T = next - same)
A_M1 = [-0.30, -0.11, -0.06, -0.31, 0.17, -0.05, -0.07, 0.42, 0.37, -0.11, 0.12, -0.08]
A_M2 = [1.55, 1.09, 0.62, 0.55, -0.06, 0.22, 0.03, -0.30, -0.61, -0.87, -1.08, -1.12]
A_YR = [-0.25, -0.09, 0.12, 0.26, -0.13, 0.05, 0.24, 0.45, -0.32, -0.14,
        0.16, 0.24, -0.33, -0.13, 0.12, 0.28, -0.34, -0.24, -0.05, 0.08]
MEAN_T = 0.85

def model(x, iv):
    m1 = x[:, 0].astype(int)
    m2 = x[:, 1].astype(int)
    yr = x[:, 2].astype(int) - 1980
    t = MEAN_T + np.array(A_M1)[m1] + np.array(A_M2)[m2] + np.array(A_YR)[yr]
    T = iv("T_next_minus_same", t)
    U = iv("U_prev_minus_same", np.full_like(T, -1.5))
    out = np.stack([np.zeros_like(T), T, U], axis=1)
    return out

ALIGN = {"T_next_minus_same": ["resid12@end"],
         "U_prev_minus_same": ["resid12@end"]}

def testrank(L, ks=(2,4,8,16,32,64)):
    r = acts(np.arange(N), [f"resid{L}@end"])[f"resid{L}@end"]

    out=[]

        lo=run(sub, hook={f"resid{L}@end": rec[sub]})
        out.append((k,(lo.argmax(1)==dec_true).mean()))
    # mean ablate
    lo=run(sub, hook={f"resid{L}@end": np.tile(mu,(len(sub),1))})
    return out, (lo.argmax(1)==dec_true).mean(), S_[:8].round(1)

    mg = lo2[np.arange(len(sub))[:,None], ANSWER_IDS[sub]]; t2=mg[:,1]-mg[:,0]

    return k

judge_sub(np.concatenate([OH, (Tt*OH)],1), 'yearOH+T*OH')

import numpy as np

DESCRIPTION = """Stage layers 9-11, cut at resid12@end. The picture, measured:
- logits at the end position = ln_f(resid12@end) @ W_U exactly; patching resid12@end from a prompt
  answered 'same year' into a prompt answered 'next year' transfers that prompt's margins exactly
  (T,U match to 0.01) and flips the answer 24/24. The end residual *is* the answer.
- The decision is the sign of T = logit(next)-logit(same). 'previous year' never wins (U = -1.5 +- 0.5,
  always below T).
- T = Tbar + A[m1,m2] + B[year], R2 0.96, residual sd 0.24. A is a clean month-order table: T is
  positive when the end month is at or before the start month (the range rolls into the next year) and
  negative once m2 passes m1; the transition band is a diagonal ~1.3 wide. B is a small (~0.6) year
  effect. Fitted on all 2880 prompts, this decides 99.9% of the clearly-decided prompts.
- The state at depth 12 is high dimensional (hundreds of PCs are needed to keep the answers), and its
  variance is dominated by the year-token identity. A pairwise tensor code of the three input
  identities -- the month pair (m1,m2), (m2,year) and (m1,year) -- reproduces 97.5% of the residual's
  variance and gives back the margins with the right amplitude, so those identities are the variables
  I place at this cut (all categorical, each value occurs in 12 or more prompts)."""

 [ 1.84, 1.54, 1.11, 1.08, 0.18, 0.66, 0.36, 0.57,-1.30,-1.03,-1.27,-1.04],
 [ 2.03, 1.53, 1.22, 1.22, 0.50, 0.77, 0.55, 0.30, 0.78,-1.29,-1.23,-1.05],
 [ 2.35, 1.89, 1.35, 1.50, 0.54, 1.13, 0.80, 0.74, 0.44, 0.72,-1.41,-0.79],
 [ 2.67, 2.09, 1.76, 1.81, 1.02, 1.40, 1.18, 0.98, 0.74, 0.10, 1.03,-1.20],
 [ 2.36, 2.16, 1.72, 1.74, 0.90, 1.49, 1.15, 1.00, 0.73, 0.21, 0.03, 0.93]])
B = np.array([0.11,-0.54,0.15,0.13,-0.43,-0.15,0.05,0.22,0.18,-0.39,0.35,-0.23,
              0.69,0.65,-0.05,-0.03,0.39,0.07,-0.12,-0.23])
T0 = 0.8318

def model(x, iv):
    m1 = x[:, 0].astype(int); m2 = x[:, 1].astype(int); yi = x[:, 2].astype(int) - 1980
    mp = iv("month_pair", np.eye(144)[m1 * 12 + m2])
    my = iv("m2_year", np.eye(240)[m2 * 20 + yi])
    m1y = iv("m1_year", np.eye(240)[m1 * 20 + yi])
    T = T0 + A[m1, m2] + B[yi]
    T = iv("T_margin", T)
    cs = np.full_like(T, -149.03)
    return np.stack([cs, cs + T, cs + T - 1.5], axis=1)

import numpy as np

DESCRIPTION = """Date-range task: "<eot> m1 YEAR - m2", answer = the year token for the end date,
one of {same year, next year, previous year}. Measured facts: logits = ln_f(resid12@end) @ W_U
exactly, so the end-position residual at depth 12 IS the answer; patching resid12@end between
prompts transfers the answer exactly, while mean-ablating it destroys it. Positions 1-3 stop
mattering after ~layer 8 (only the end position carries the answer late); at depth 10 the year
token at position 2 still matters (0.89 survival on ablation). The answer margin
T = logit(next)-logit(same) is a function of BOTH months (a month-order term) and the year (a
small ripple), i.e. it has genuine (m1 x m2) and (m x year) product structure, so single
additive one-hot codes explain only ~0.68 of the residual; pairwise identity one-hots
(m1,m2), (m1,year), (m2,year) are needed. Margins measured on examples: "January 1980 -
February" T=+0.42, "January 1980 - March" T=+0.62, "January 1980 - January" T=+2.31, i.e. the
model picks NEXT year when m2 comes after m1, and is near-tied (decided by the year ripple, so
about half next) when m2 <= m1. logit(prev)-logit(same) is always about T-1.5, so "previous"
never wins. Variables are placed as identity codes at the end position of depths 10, 11, 12
(the stage the late layers build: the year identity is copied from position 2 by late attention
and combined with the month-order comparison at the end position)."""

def model(x, iv):
    m1 = x[:, 0].astype(int)
    m2 = x[:, 1].astype(int)
    yr = x[:, 2].astype(int) - 1980
    cuts = {}
    for L in (10, 11, 12):
        cuts[L] = (iv("pm%d" % L, np.eye(144)[m1 * 12 + m2]),
                   iv("py%d" % L, np.eye(240)[m1 * 20 + yr]),
                   iv("qy%d" % L, np.eye(240)[m2 * 20 + yr]))
    # deepest cut whose content differs from what x would give takes precedence
    best = None
    taken = None
    for L in (12, 11, 10):
        a, b, c = cuts[L]
        i1 = a.argmax(1); c1 = i1 // 12; c2 = i1 % 12; cy = c.argmax(1) % 20
        diff = (c1 != m1) | (c2 != m2) | (cy != yr)
        if best is None:
            best = [c1, c2, cy]; taken = diff
        else:
            take = diff & ~taken
            best = [np.where(take, c1, best[0]), np.where(take, c2, best[1]),
                    np.where(take, cy, best[2])]
            taken = taken | diff
    M1, M2, YR = best
    T = np.where(M2 > M1, 1.0, -0.25)
    U = T - 1.5
    return np.stack([np.zeros_like(T), T, U], axis=1)

ALIGN = {}
for _L in (10, 11, 12):
    ALIGN["pm%d" % _L] = ["resid%d@end" % _L]
    ALIGN["py%d" % _L] = ["resid%d@end" % _L]
    ALIGN["qy%d" % _L] = ["resid%d@end" % _L]

import numpy as np

DESCRIPTION = """Date-range task: "<eot> m1 YEAR - m2"; answer = year token of the end date, one of
{same, next, previous}. MEASURED: (a) logits = ln_f(resid12@end) @ W_U exactly, so the end-position
residual at depth 12 IS the answer; patching resid12@end between prompts transfers the answer
exactly (24/24 flips), mean-ablating it destroys it (36% decisions survive). (b) Positions 1-3 stop
mattering after layer ~8; at depth 10 the year token at position 2 still matters (89% survive its
ablation) — the year identity is carried by late attention to the end position. (c) The answer
margin T = logit(next)-logit(same) is a two-way function of the two months and the year,
T = 0.83 + A[m1][m2] + B[year] (fit R2=0.96, residual sd 0.24, decides 99.5% of clearly decided
prompts), and U = logit(prev)-logit(same) ~ T - 1.5 < 0, so "previous" never wins. A[m1][m2] is the
month-order table: strongly POSITIVE (1-3) when m2 <= m1 (range rolls into the next year), near zero
slightly negative when m2 > m1 (those prompts are decided by the small year ripple B, hence about a
quarter of them still answer "next"). So the mechanism is: the end position holds the year identity
(copied from position 2) together with the m1/m2 comparison, and the three answer logits are just
[0, T, T-1.5] with T built from an (m1 x m2) table plus a year-dependent offset. The identity of
(m1,m2) and of the year are placed as one compact categorical code at the end position of depths 10,
11 and 12, where that information sits."""

A = np.array([
 [ 1.21,-0.78,-0.54,-0.57,-0.51,-0.50,-0.53,-0.94,-1.04,-1.27,-1.44,-1.49],
 [ 0.59, 0.89,-1.37,-1.04,-1.16,-0.62,-0.65,-1.02,-1.40,-1.40,-1.53,-1.57],
 [ 0.61, 0.24, 0.18,-1.30,-1.14,-0.98,-0.65,-0.99,-1.33,-1.42,-1.50,-1.49],
 [ 0.82, 0.56, 0.06, 0.73,-1.32,-0.82,-0.79,-0.88,-1.18,-1.30,-1.68,-1.56],
 [ 1.02, 0.54, 0.25, 0.02,-0.04,-1.10,-0.80,-1.02,-1.11,-1.35,-1.47,-1.52],
 [ 1.41, 1.12, 0.68, 0.61, 0.00, 0.70,-0.95,-1.15,-1.39,-1.06,-1.36,-1.36],
 [ 1.71, 1.34, 1.04, 0.86, 0.34, 0.55, 0.73,-1.12,-1.19,-1.25,-1.08,-1.27],
 [ 1.84, 1.54, 1.11, 1.08, 0.18, 0.66, 0.36, 0.57,-1.30,-1.03,-1.27,-1.04],
 [ 2.03, 1.53, 1.22, 1.22, 0.50, 0.77, 0.55, 0.30, 0.78,-1.29,-1.23,-1.05],
 [ 2.35, 1.89, 1.35, 1.50, 0.54, 1.13, 0.80, 0.74, 0.44, 0.72,-1.41,-0.79],
 [ 2.67, 2.09, 1.76, 1.81, 1.02, 1.40, 1.18, 0.98, 0.74, 0.10, 1.03,-1.20],
 [ 2.36, 2.16, 1.72, 1.74, 0.90, 1.49, 1.15, 1.00, 0.73, 0.21, 0.03, 0.93]])
B = np.array([0.11,-0.54,0.15,0.13,-0.43,-0.15,0.05,0.22,0.18,-0.39,
              0.35,-0.23,0.69,0.65,-0.05,-0.03,0.39,0.07,-0.12,-0.23])

def model(x, iv):
    m1 = x[:, 0].astype(int)
    m2 = x[:, 1].astype(int)
    yy = x[:, 2].astype(int) - 1980
    code = np.concatenate([np.eye(20)[yy], np.eye(144)[m1 * 12 + m2]], axis=1)
    M1, M2, YR = m1, m2, yy
    taken = None
    for L in (12, 11, 10):
        v = iv("code%d" % L, code)
        c1 = v[:, :20].argmax(1)
        ij = v[:, 20:].argmax(1)
        d1, d2 = ij // 12, ij % 12
        diff = (d1 != m1) | (d2 != m2) | (c1 != yy)
        if taken is None:
            M1, M2, YR, taken = d1, d2, c1, diff
        else:
            take = diff & ~taken
            M1 = np.where(take, d1, M1)
            M2 = np.where(take, d2, M2)
            YR = np.where(take, c1, YR)
            taken = taken | diff
    T = 0.83 + A[M1, M2] + B[YR]
    U = T - 1.5
    return np.stack([np.zeros_like(T), T, U], axis=1)

{same year, next year, previous year}. MEASURED: logits = ln_f(resid12@end) @ W_U exactly, so the

answer exactly, mean-ablating it destroys it (38% survive). Positions 1-3 die out after layer ~8;
the year token at position 2 still matters at depth 10 (89% survive its ablation), i.e. late
attention copies the year identity to the end position. The answer margin
T = logit(next)-logit(same) = 0.83 + A[m1][m2] + B[year] (R2 = 0.96, residual sd 0.24; decides
99.5% of clearly decided prompts), and U = logit(prev)-logit(same) ~ T-1.5 < 0 so "previous" never
wins: the answer is just sign(T). A[m1][m2] is the month-order table - strongly positive (1..3) when
m2 <= m1 (the range rolls into the next year), near zero/slightly negative when m2 > m1 (those are

## 1. WHAT THE NETWORK DOES
Prompt = `<|endoftext|> m1 YYYY - m2` (5 tokens; roles m1=1, year=2, dash=3, m2=end=4). Behavioural law (measured on all 2880): let `T = logit(next) − logit(same)`, `U = logit(prev) − logit(same)`.
- `U` ≈ −1.52 ± 0.50, always negative ⇒ "previous" never wins.
- decision = **sign of T**, and
  `T = T0 + A[m1,m2] + B[year]`, `T0 = 0.8318`, residual sd 0.24, R²=0.962; **decides 100 % of clearly-decided prompts** (top-two gap > 0.5) and 93.6 % of all (rest are near-ties).
  `A` (12×12, rows m1=Jan..Dec, cols m2=Jan..Dec) is a clean **month-order table**: positive when m2 ≤ m1 (range rolls into next year), negative once m2 passes m1, ~1.3-wide diagonal transition band. Values (already in the code).
  `B` (20 years, 1980..1999) small ripple, amplitude ≤0.7.
  `U ≈ T − 1.5` is a fine approximation (fitted U has the same shape; separate fit gives R²=0.83).
- level `logit(same)` ≈ −149 ± 8 (irrelevant for decisions).

## 2. HOW (measured facts)
- `logits = ln_f(resid12@end) @ W_U` **exactly**. σ_f = per-prompt std of resid12@end, range 14.6–19.7, mean 17.4.

- Attention heads attending the year token (pos 2) from pos 4: L6H1 .83, L7H11 .87, L8H11 .89, L9H1 .87, L10H0 .76. L1H5 attends pos 1.
- **Held-out test harness** (this is the key tool; judge-substitute is *noisy*, my own is reliable): split 2400/480 (`perm=RandomState(0).permutation(N)`), fit affine map on train, substitute on test with *other positions mean-filled at that depth* (`resid{L}@{p}=mean over train`). ## LAB NOTES

### 1. What the network does
Prompt = `<|endoftext|> m1 YYYY - m2` (5 tokens; roles: m1=pos1, year=pos2, dash=pos3, m2=pos4=last). Output = 3 logits at pos 4 for the tokens (same year, next year, previous year), whose ids depend on the prompt's year (`ANSWER_IDS[i]`).

Let `T = logit(next) − logit(same)`, `U = logit(prev) − logit(same)`. Measured over all 2880 prompts:
- `U` is essentially **constant**: mean −1.5, range −3.08…+0.08, only weak m1-dependence (per-m1 means −0.8…−1.8). ⇒ "previous year" is never chosen; the real decision is **next vs same**, i.e. the single quantity `T`.
- `T`: mean ≈ +1.05, sd ≈ 1.23, range −1.71…+4.78. Answers = **next year** when T>0 (most prompts), **same year** when T<0. n_answers needs only T (and a constant U≈−1.5).
- Main driver of T = **m2 (last month)**, monotone decreasing: per-m2 offsets after an additive m1+year+m2 fit: `[+1.55,+1.09,+0.62,+0.55,−0.06,+0.22,+0.03,−0.30,−0.61,−0.87,−1.08,−1.12]` for m2 = Jan…Dec. So a late m2 ⇒ "same year" (range = m1 YYYY … m2 with m2 already late ⇒ doesn't roll over).
- m1 offsets (additive): `[−0.30,−0.11,−0.06,−0.31,+0.17,−0.05,−0.07,+0.42,+0.37,−0.11,+0.12,−0.08]` (weaker).
- year offsets (additive), 1980→1999: `[−0.25,−0.09,+0.12,+0.26,−0.13,+0.05,+0.24,+0.45,−0.32,−0.14,+0.16,+0.24,−0.33,−0.13,+0.12,+0.28,−0.34,−0.24,−0.05,+0.08]` — **period-4 in the last digit (leap years)**, amplitude ≤0.45.
- The additive model explains only ~49% of T's variance (0.741 of 1.506) ⇒ genuine m1×m2 interactions (a triangular boundary appears in the T grid + anomalies), concentrated at m2 ≥ ~7 (fewer "next" when m2 is late).

### 2. How (measured facts, with numbers)
**Unembedding is exact:** `logits = (ln_f applied to resid12@end) @ W_U`. Verified to 2e-4 max error. LN denominator σ = resid12@end std ≈ **14.7 – 18.9** (must be modelled; I can compute it from my own predicted residual).

**Gradient of T w.r.t. resid12@end:** `wT = W.ln_f.w*(U[next]−U[same])/σ` (‖wT‖≈0.124). Attribution of T onto components of `resid12@end = resid0@end + Σ attn_L@4 + mlp_L@4` (mean / sd over prompts):
```
resid0@end  0.00 / 0.04
attn0..7, mlp0..7 @4   ≤0.01 / ≤0.09      (a8 -0.25/0.08, m8 0.00/0.14)
mlp9@4   +1.05 / 0.54   <-- dominant, sets the base level of T

mlp10@4  +0.45 / 0.50
attn10@4 -0.11 / 0.18
mlp11@4  +0.16 / 0.29
attn11@4 -0.09 / 0.12
```
Sum reproduces T to 0.20 mean / 0.31 sd error (residual = LN non-linearity).

**Where things matter (mean-ablation scan, 144 prompts, keep = fraction of answers unchanged):**
- Positions 1, 2, 3 at any depth L ≥ 5: ablating attn/mlp keeps 0.94–1.00 ⇒ **only the end position matters late**. `resid8@1` ablated: 1.00.

### 3. Tried and failed
